extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students, and scientists interested in philosophy and history of science (theory change, paradigms)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying evaluative criteria for when scientific work constitutes crisis, extraordinary research, or a paradigm shift (scientific revolution). Focuses on symptoms, mechanisms, and conceptual consequences of paradigm change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of thought experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytical thought-experimentation exposes the old paradigm to existing knowledge in ways that isolate the root of crisis unattainable in the laboratory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought experiments (as used by Galileo, Einstein, Bohr, etc.) are especially calculated to reveal contradictions between a paradigm and known results; they may be deployed singly or together with other extraordinary procedures to prepare the scientific mind to recognize anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis as catalyst for discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentration of scientific attention on a narrow area of trouble and preparedness to recognize anomalies often proliferates new discoveries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awareness of crisis distinguishes cases (e.g., Lavoisier’s work on oxygen from Priestley’s, late-19th/early-20th-century optical and quantum discoveries). Discoveries may be accidental, predictions of a new hypothesis (which help transform it into a paradigm), or previously assimilated effects newly reinterpreted once anomaly is noticed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symptoms of transition to extraordinary research
rubrics_metrics.description: The transition from normal to extraordinary research is signaled by the proliferation of competing articulations, a willingness to try anything, explicit expression of discontent, and recourse to philosophy and debate over fundamentals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These behaviors are indicators of a breakdown in normal scientific activity and are more diagnostic for identifying crisis than the mere occurrence of revolutions; their presence, not just formal revolution, helps define normal vs extraordinary science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of scientific revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific revolutions are non-cumulative developmental episodes in which an older paradigm is replaced in whole or in part by an incompatible new one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This replacement is analogous in significant respects to political revolutions: both are inaugurated by a growing sense of malfunction in existing institutions and both may require partial relinquishment of an old institutional (or conceptual) framework in favor of a new one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of malfunction as prerequisite for revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: A growing sense that existing paradigms have ceased to function adequately (often confined to a subdivision of the community) is prerequisite to crisis and thus to revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like political revolutions, the sense of malfunction emerges within a segment of the community and leads to polarization between defenders of the old paradigm and proponents of alternatives; initial estrangement and eccentric behavior precede concrete proposals for reconstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community assent and persuasive argumentation in paradigm choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Because paradigms are circular (each side uses its own paradigm to defend itself), paradigm choice cannot be settled by logic and experiment alone; assent of the relevant scientific community based on persuasive argumentation is decisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments grounded in a paradigm can powerfully exhibit what scientific practice under that paradigm would be like and thus persuade; however, no higher logical standard exists to compel conversion of those who refuse to 'step into the circle.' Studying revolution therefore requires examining techniques of persuasion effective within scientific communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anomalies as triggers for new theories
rubrics_metrics.description: New theories are called forth primarily by recognized anomalies whose stubborn refusal to be assimilated to existing paradigms forces reconsideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are three classes of phenomena: (1) those well explained by existing paradigms (rarely yield new theories); (2) those indicated by paradigms but requiring further articulation; (3) recognized anomalies that resist assimilation — only the third gives rise to new theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive difference criterion for theory replacement
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful new theory must permit predictions different from those of its predecessor; such predictive differences are the marks of genuine incompatibility and displacement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the successor theory resolves anomalies the predecessor could not, it must change some predictions; historical examples include the role of rejecting caloric theory before energy conservation could be assimilated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment to a paradigm required for normal science
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal (cumulative) research depends on commitment to a paradigm, including commitments that extend beyond full precedent, in order to generate puzzles and guide instrument design and problem selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricting a theory’s legitimate applicability only to previously demonstrated ranges (a strict positivist stance) would prohibit scientists from using theories in new areas or at greater precision and would thus halt the mechanism that produces surprises, anomalies, and crises — the drivers of fundamental change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual incommensurability and reinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent derivations of an older theory as a special case of a newer one are spurious unless one reinterprets the fundamental concepts; the meanings of shared terms often change between paradigms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: deriving Newtonian laws from Einsteinian mechanics by limiting parameters still leaves the variables carrying Einsteinian referents (space, time, mass). To call the derived statements 'Newton’s Laws' requires redefining terms — demonstrating that conceptual change, not mere limiting-case mathematics, characterizes revolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm differences: substance, methods, and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Successive paradigms differ not only about substantive claims concerning the population and behavior of the universe but also about methods, problem-fields, and standards distinguishing scientific solutions from speculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reception of a new paradigm often redefines the corresponding science: some former problems may become unscientific, while previously trivial questions may become central; standards for what counts as a real scientific solution change, producing incommensurability between traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of youth/novices in paradigm innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental inventors of new paradigms have often been very young or relatively new to the field and thus less committed to traditional rules of normal science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because they are less committed by prior practice, they are particularly likely to see that traditional rules no longer define a playable game and to conceive replacements; empirical support is impressionistic and requires systematic investigation (e.g., Lehman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism generating unanticipated novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal research chooses problems solvable with existing conceptual and instrumental techniques; unanticipated novelty (new discoveries or theories) emerges only when anticipations and instruments prove wrong, and often the importance of the discovery is proportional to the stubbornness of the anomaly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why cumulative acquisition of novelty is rare: science progresses normally by solving problems within a paradigm; only persistent anomalies push toward invention of new theories. Excessive focus on immediately useful problems (regardless of relation to existing knowledge) can inhibit development.
